We tend to each other’s wounds, and we sing Chardi Kala, our community’s resolve to remain cheerful in struggle.

To me, the greatest beauty of this community model is the unbreakable spirit it produces. Alone, one’s flicker of hope is inevitably extinguished. Together, however, we can keep the flame alive, sharing the communal embers when our personal supply runs short.

To overcome the behemoth that is the factory farm industry, I believe the animal rights movement must replicate aspects of this spiritual community. We need community centers to facilitate deep and multi-generational relationships, grand narratives to root us in a shared past and future, and a cohesive identity to unite us in struggle. Veganism is as close as the animal rights movement gets to this, but nowhere has veganism produced a unity comparable to that of the Sikh community. In my hometown of Phoenix, for example, we have three Sikh temples, but zero animal rights centers. These temples draw hundreds of people each week, while our grassroots animal rights group draws perhaps five. I dream of a world where animal activists congregate in a fashion and fervor rivaling that of organized religion. This might seem like a pipe dream, but I know this world to be possible because prior social movements have already accomplished the task. (See Quakers in the abolitionist movement; the black church in the civil rights movement; and ashrams in India’s independence movement).

I believe the animal rights movement to be uniquely fit for this spiritual community, as few journeys are as meaningful as our own. Our mission is to alleviate trillions of sentient beings from torment and suffering, unleashing human compassion on a scale that the world has never before seen. This is an epic story waiting to be told. We must see that it is written.

So, what does the future hold? On a personal level, I am admittedly uncertain. I may very well be convicted and incarcerated before the year’s end. Collectively, however, I have deep confidence that our movement—our species—will triumph over the great evil that is factory farming. The day will come where every slaughterhouse shutters its doors, and humanity will meet its fellow creatures, no longer with chains and knives, but soft hands and open arms.

WHAT’S NEXT!

  • Potluck at Dolores Park on Saturday at 1pm! To my Bay Area brethren, come through to our potluck this Saturday. We’ll share good food, hangout with dogs, and discuss emerging political opportunities. Our Partiful already has 50+ RSVPs. I hope to see you all there!

  • Community Event at the Phoenix Gurdwara on Saturday, August 1st! I still need to create an event page for this, but save the date! I’m trying to get 100+ members of our Sikh, Indian, and pro-animal communities to converge upon the Gurdwara I was raised in. We’ll discuss how my case fits into the history of religious resistance, and we’ll sit down for “langar,” the Sikh practice of communal eating.

  • Enjoy today!

item.title: What is love?
item.description: To me, love is presence. Love is emptying oneself, such that your entire world becomes nothing but their eyes, their voice, their emotion.
item.content:encoded:
By Taj Uppal

To me, love is presence. Love is emptying oneself, such that your entire world becomes nothing but their eyes, their voice, their emotion. Love is the act of holding this space for another—a pure and undivided attention.

I’m rarely able to cultivate this presence, as I’m often preoccupied with stressors and anxieties. In the moments where I am truly present before another, though, I am in awe. I am struck by the beauty and depth of the person before me. The recognition that their world is just as complex as my own; the understanding that no one on planet earth is quite like them. I am then overwhelmed with gratitude, because what a gift it is to be present before this person. To seem them for everything they are, at least for this moment.

I’m not adequately describing the feeling. Presence before another is like realizing that every scribble is the Mona Lisa; every hum, the Moonlight Sonata. Presence is the thief of boredom, because no one is boring when you truly gaze upon their soul.

For me, eye contact and physical touch amplify this presence, which is probably why my deepest experiences are often with romantic partners. Presence, after all, is an intimate experience, and you can only gaze into your brother’s eyes for so long. Still, presence—presence as an expression of love—is something that can be shared in almost any context. It’s strange to be making this comparison, but beyond my romantic partners, perhaps the deepest presence I’ve felt is that of bearing witness to suffering. Suffering, even when observed behind the safety of a screen, feels so consuming. I am most moved by the imagery of animals in slaughterhouses, and when I fully surrender my presence to these poor souls, everything else melts away, and I feel as if I am left with nothing but the truth—the truth being the depth, the severity, the gravity, of their suffering. To share a fragment of their experience is to share my love.

I also want to discuss presence in the context of friendship. I believe the deepest forms of friendship require such presence. Because if you view someone as a means—a means to higher status, achieving a work-related goal, even exploring a hobby—then the relationship can only get so deep. True connection requires an understanding that the person before you is whole in their own right. That their life contains an infinite depth of complexity. That you are merely a side-character in the great drama that is their life story. I believe that it is upon this recognition that we are truly able to see and connect with others. Without this dissolution, our egos crowd the space between.

To cultivate these connections with the people in my life, I’ve found curiosity to be the strongest catalyst. This curiosity is, at its core, the yearning to know who is the person before me. In practice, curiosity primarily manifests as the act of listening. But it is also all the little things: follow-up questions to delve deeper, texting a week later to receive an update, and remembering the details, so as to call back upon them. Curiosity also requires a degree of inner, self-work, because attention is a finite resource, and insecurity directs inwards what might otherwise be directed outwards. There’s no simple solution to this problem of insecurity, but one simple trick I often use is breathing between spaces. Before I enter a house party, for example, I’ll bring my attention to my breath for just a minute. This centers me, allowing my attention, curiosity, and presence to flow outwards.

When it comes to political organizing, a genuine presence is extremely critical, as politics easily instrumentalizes people towards an external goal. Electoral politics, for example, is infamously transactional. But even when it comes to grassroots movements, it is not uncommon for new activists to feel burned by senior organizers. “You pretended to be my friend, just so I would help your cause!” These allegations often ring true.

Here, again, I believe the solution is a genuine presence. The organizer must recognize the intrinsic worth of every organizational member. They must take the time to pause and understand; to listen and to see. If conducted authentically, this presence will be felt and replicated throughout the community. It will carve deep and meaningful relationships, transforming what would otherwise be a transactional group of coworkers into a spiritual community of believers. In turn, this community will form the capacity to overcome great struggle—struggle that would have been insurmountable in isolation.

This is the vision I hold for the animal rights movement and the world. I dream of a beloved community of mutual listeners. A world where presence—the seeing of another’s soul—is abundantly, freely, joyfully exchanged. That’s love!

WHAT’S NEXT?

  • On Monday, August 24th, at 1pm, I’ll be returning to my alma mater, Berkeley Law, to tell my story from law student to felony defendant. I’d love to see you there, and please message me if you’re interested!

  • On August 25th, I have my pretrial hearing in Kings County. I’m not sure what to expect here, but at the very least my felony grand theft charge should be reduced to a misdemeanor, as this felony charge was unlawful from the start!

  • Sometime in September (perhaps September 1st), I’ll be speaking at ASU Law! Come through and we might just gaze into each other’s souls, forming a beloved community with the capacity to free trillions of our fellow creatures from torment and suffering ahaa…

item.title: Between Two Worlds
item.description: A year ago, I moved home to be closer to family, my Nani especially.
item.content:encoded:
By Taj Uppal

A year ago, I moved home to be closer to family, my Nani especially. She has late-stage Alzheimer’s, and, in a very real sense, I knew it was now or never. Never wasn’t an outcome I could accept, so, in September, I packed my belongings and said goodbye to Oakland. My home is now the guest bedroom at Nani’s—the Phoenix suburbs where I was raised.

The last year here has been a bit of everything: joyful and sorrowful, peaceful but chaotic, meaningful yet mundane. The juxtaposition is heightened by my circumstances, where I am simultaneously a homebound grandson and a multi-felony defendant. These worlds do not mesh easily, and the hardest part of the last year has been navigating the space between.

I moved home because I wanted to excel in the first of these worlds—the world where I fulfill my family’s expectations, where I serve them to my fullest capacity. I wanted to care for Nani, dutifully and wholeheartedly, as she has always cared for me. And I wanted to mend my relationship with Papa, as the conflict over my career path has distanced us in recent years. I turned down a fellowship at Denver Law’s animal law clinic, and I pursued an associate position at a big law firm like Papa’s always wanted. Ultimately, I passed the patent bar exam and lined up a firm job, but just a week before I was slated to start, my felony charges came down.

Enter our second world, that of factory farms, sacrifice, and struggle. My job offer is revoked, and, somehow, I muster the courage to explain things. “Papa, I won’t be able to start on Monday.” We were more hopeful at the time. That we might be able to negotiate a quick plea deal; send me back to work. But five months later and the charges still loom. In the meantime, my family has learned what it means to endure the carceral system. The uncertainty, the anxiety, and the cloud that it casts.

Papa feels like I’ve betrayed him. In a sense, I have. I’ve taken the world that he’s given me—the world with all its wealth and status and opportunity—and I’ve wagered it upon a cause of which he has no concern. Papa is often, and understandably, angry that I’ve done so. But in certain moments, he reveals the love that underlies it all.

“Please don’t make yourself a martyr. You are my only son.”

I am sobbing as I write these words. Sobbing for Papa and his fears; Mama, and the knots in her stomach. I see the toll my prosecution has taken on my parents, and I so desperately want to alleviate its burden.

These are the worlds I straddle between. One that calls me to serve our family; another that calls me to serve our humanity—to rectify this great violence our species has sowed.

For five months, I’ve failed to reconcile these worlds. With no means to merge them, I am learning to sit in the uneasy space between. I’ve pleaded “not guilty” to felony charges, while Nani eats breakfast outside my bedroom. I’ve conceded my fingerprints to police officers, while Papa observes from the courtroom gallery. This experience has been a great exercise in mental fortitude, and, while I wouldn’t wish the experience upon anyone else, I do feel myself growing stronger. I am learning to remain calm amidst the storm.

I intend to continue developing this strength, deploying its force on behalf of the vulnerable and voiceless creatures of this earth. Though their suffering and their salvation lie worlds apart, I will struggle tirelessly in the space between. I will gaze upon our nation’s slaughterhouses—their screams, their cries, their bloodstained floors—and I will accept responsibility for the devastation we have wrought. At the same time, I will dream—stubbornly, wholeheartedly—of a world where the blood turns to rain, the floors cleansed of stain. I will struggle to merge what is with what may be.

Along this journey, I will inevitably commit many mistakes. I will be messy, flawed, sometimes deflated. Still, so long as I am not alone, I have the utmost confidence in my ability—our ability—to persist. Together, we will chip away at this chasm between worlds. We will close the distance in our personal lives; we will merge with the compassion that is our higher selves—our true humanity.

What’s next!

  • Later today, I’ll appear for my pretrial hearing, where, inshallah, my felony charges will be reduced to misdemeanors, as the government failed to prove felony grand theft’s $950 threshold.

  • Our Phoenix animal rights group is starting to host weekly, Saturday hangouts at vegan restaurants (shoutout Alyssa for organizing)! This weekend, we’ll be at Strip Mall at 11:30am. Come through!

item.title: Was it worth it?
item.description: A cost-benefit analysis of my civil disobedience
item.content:encoded:
By Taj Uppal

Truthfully, I’m not sure. The costs were certainly steep. As of last week, I officially lost my associate position at a large law firm. Accounting for the lost wages and my attorneys’ fees, I’m down about $80,000.

My current job search is also significantly more challenging, as each interview now requires a disclosure of my criminal record. (Since googling my name results in a headline titled “This Arizona Lawyer Faces Prison,” I figured I might as well disclose the information myself). In the last week alone, two law firms have rejected me explicitly due to my criminal record. Time will tell how significant these constraints become, but already they are real.

My career aside, the prosecution’s strain on my family was easily its greatest cost. Mama spent nights researching the prison rape rate, fearing for my incarceration. Papa, for the first time, sobbed to me over the phone. “You’ve aged us,” he said. He’s right. My prosecution—my choices—inflicted serious hardship upon the people I love. I feel really guilty about that, and I’ll have to work hard to make up for it.

The personal hardship was also a significant cost. Thankfully, I was never drowning, but the prosecution was definitely the most stressful and uncertain period of my life. The duration was the hardest part. Six months is just a long time to be in the state’s crosshairs, and the looming threat makes it hard to do anything else. My family is also very disappointed in me, and that is difficult to accept.

As for the benefits of my civil disobedience, rescuing Phoebe was definitely the most tangible outcome. Because of my own two hands, someone’s life was transformed from suffering to joy, from neglect to tender care. That is beautiful—the only thing is, I could’ve easily rescued Phoebe without going through all the trouble. Nighttime rescues of factory-farmed animals, for example, are easily conducted without detection. Worse yet, I actually paid the farmer $450—the goats’ alleged market value—to secure my case’s dismissal. That payment makes the whole operation feel quite silly, because if I was going to pay the farmer anyway, then why not just do it upfront and avoid all the trouble?

One answer to that question is that the “trouble” draws attention to the cause. That was certainly true in my case. Over the last six months, I’ve racked up 1.5 million views on Instagram and grown to 10k followers. That’s pretty cool, but honestly, in the world of social media influencers, these are absolute rookie numbers. As just one reference point, vegan influencer Danny Ishay has generated seven million views in the last month alone. That is more than 25 times my productivity; no dramatic sacrifice required.

Beyond social media, I’ve written some decent blogs, spoken on podcasts, and generated local news articles. Most excitingly, I have a national CBS piece dropping soon. Hopefully that performs well, but still, the attention around my case has overall been quite small.

One saving grace may be that, although small in quantity, the attention around my case has been of special quality. Your average vegan influencer, for example, is not as inspiring as the freedom-risking, freedom fighter. I feel quite confident in that assertion, and yet this is also where my cost-benefit analysis starts to break down. I have no reliable measure of how “inspired” people are by my sacrifice. I have certain proxies—for example, (1) the ~100 people who told me they feel inspired, (2) the surge of activity within the vegan society I organize, and (3) the four law schools I’ve been invited to speak at. These proxies certainly speak to my credibility boost, but they’re not the best measure of impact. I’m uncertain how any of this ultimately helps animals.

I suppose this strikes at the fundamental issue of civil disobedience tactics: measurability. Unlike a corporate cage-free campaign where you can more-or-less calculate the campaign’s cost-effectiveness, civil disobedience is a tactic that relies almost entirely on its second-order effects. How much dialogue was generated? How many activists were seeded? How much culture was changed? Measuring these outcomes is difficult, and, in my case, the answer is probably “not much.”

That sucks, but at the very least, what I can say for sure is that my personal growth has been enormous. For the last six months, I’ve been under immense pressure from not only the government, but also my family and sometimes my fellow activists. Withstanding that pressure has not been easy, but I stayed true regardless. Under the threat of incarceration and the unraveling of my career, I refused to fold on my beliefs, spoke before hundreds of people, and am soon to become a national news story. That has given me great confidence that I can do hard things. Truly, I feel stronger, clearer, and more grounded than ever before. I’ll write more on this in my next blog, but the short of it is that facing felonies is an excellent character building exercise!

Summary of Costs and Benefits

Looking at this table, I am far from convinced that my civil disobedience was worth it, especially considering that rescuing Phoebe and garnering attention are achievable without the self-sacrifice. If anything, my family turmoil probably tips the scales in favor of the costs.

Still, I would do it again. Perhaps that is crazy and irrational, and perhaps I am a terrible son for dragging my family into this self-inflicted struggle. Seriously, I feel guilty even writing the words, but I am willing to roll the dice. That is the person I want to be. I refuse to live a normal life while this great moral atrocity unfolds. I don’t want to just write blogs and file lawsuits and pursue a career path. I want to do something that truly captures the moral gravity of what is at stake, and nothing will ever communicate that more aptly than sacrifice. I believe this sacrifice holds great transformative power, and I intend to harness its potential on behalf of the more vulnerable creatures of this earth. Nothing moves me more than their suffering.

item.title: True wealth
item.description: Relationships are the most precious treasure on planet earth. That was the most important lesson I learned from my six months of prosecution.
item.content:encoded:
By Taj Uppal

Relationships are the most precious treasure on planet earth. That was the most important lesson I learned from my six months of prosecution.

During this period, a lot fell out from under me. I lost my job at a large law firm. My family relationships became very strained. And I faced the loss of both my career and my freedom. That was really hard and scary, but I still managed to live a happy and meaningful life in the meantime. Maintaining that mindset was only possible due to the strength of my relationships. My family was a double-edged sword in this regard, serving as both stressor and support. My friendships, however, were a literal lifeline—the web that caught me when my other foundations crumbled.

In practice, this web was woven with the simplest of materials: check-ins, phone calls, showing up when it mattered. I felt this most strongly at my Gurdwara event here in Phoenix. Dozens of uncles, aunties, and friends showed out to listen to my story, to pray for my wellbeing. As we stood for Ardas, I felt such a certainty that everything would be okay. Not because I knew my case would resolve favorably, but because I knew my people were behind me regardless. That is love, and it is the truest wealth that there is. Yes, I was facing two felonies, but I was also gathered in a room full of loved ones. I wouldn’t trade that for the world.

That feeling of community is irreplaceable. It’s this deep sense of security—this certainty that, even if the worst comes to bear, I’ll be okay. I’ll be okay because I will never be alone.

I feel like our society doesn’t value relationships enough, friendships especially. As just one example of this devaluation, Papa is constantly urging me to move back to San Francisco to work in big law. He has a point: San Francisco has more jobs, and big law offers a starting salary of $225k. One of the reasons I don’t want to move back, though, is because I just signed a lease in Phoenix with my best friend Arun. When I explained that to Papa, he was incredulous that a friendship would weigh against a career move. What Papa doesn’t understand, though, is how much Arun means to me. It’s definitely gay to be writing about Arun like this, but he really is my anchor. We’ve been friends for more than ten years now, and he’s probably the number one reason I didn’t spiral while being prosecuted. That is a gift that no amount of money or prestige will ever provide.

The Harvard Happiness Project, the longest-running study on human happiness, supports this idea. After following hundreds of men for nearly 80 years, the study found that close relationships—more than wealth or prestige—were the strongest predictor of long term health and happiness. As the study’s director summarized, “The good life is built with good relationships.”

I wish our society was built more around this wisdom. I wish that more of my friends lived in the same city, that we had more third spaces to bump into each other, that we spent more time together in-person. College is perhaps the institution best at providing these opportunities, while adult life is rather lacking in its social infrastructure. We should really work on that. Let’s design our lives such that community is the default, such that we run into each other by accident.

Our social norms are also due for an update. I feel that so many of us are misled to believe that money and prestige will provide the security we seek. They won’t. This is a trap. Money and prestige are of course powerful tools, but they are entirely incapable of filling the holes in our hearts. Only relationships—only love—can do that.

Just as relationships are the foundation of a healthy life, relationships are also the foundation of a healthy social movement. Relationships allow for greater coordination and efficacy, provide security to those who bear the movement’s greatest costs, and maintain resolve in the face of longstanding, grand challenges. The organizer’s role is to create the conditions for these relationships to blossom and flourish. Equally important is the ability to resolve the conflict that inevitably arises from these relationships. Social movements live or die by their ability to maintain healthy relationships.

I give the animal rights movement a C in its relationship infrastructure. We don’t deserve an F because we at least have the vegan identity, vegan restaurants, grassroots groups, some professional networks, some conferences, some shared media, and a constellation of loosely coordinating nonprofits. Still, this infrastructure needs to be much stronger, and we remain almost entirely lacking in community centers, grand narratives, shared rituals, multi-generational relationships, youth programs, campus organizing, student-to-professional pipelines, and, perhaps most importantly, an agreed-upon goal. I’m confident that our movement infrastructure activates less than 1% of the latent energy that exists for animals. Just one data point to support this assertion is that, two years ago, 36% of voters in Denver voted to ban slaughterhouses. Can’t we get more of these people to do something?

Building this relationship infrastructure is, in my view, our movement’s most pressing task at hand. This infrastructure will foster the relationships that sustain the action that inspire the change. Also, as it turns out, this relationship building exercise is the key to living a happy and meaningful life, so it’s sort of a win-win!
